strap: A daily dispatch from the world you are entering

lead.title: Carlyle has hired two senior executives to lead its family office business and set a target of USD 200 billion in new capital by 2028, after putting the addressable market for family offices at USD 5 trillion
lead.standfirst: The appointment of a former BlackRock relationship head and a family office veteran from Cercano Management shows how seriously the largest alternative asset managers now treat the family office as a client in its own right, rather than as an occasional co-investor.
lead.body:
Carlyle announced on 25 September that David Seeberan has joined as partner and global head of its family office group, moving from Cercano Management, the firm built around the fortune of Microsoft co-founder Paul Allen and dedicated to ultra wealthy individuals and family foundations. Seeberan is based in San Francisco and reports to Jeff Nedelman and Amal Alibhai. Alongside him, Victoria Matthews joins as managing director for Europe and Asia from BlackRock, where she managed the firm's relationships with family offices and endowments across the United Kingdom, and will work out of London.

The hires sit on top of a strategy Carlyle has been building since 2023, when it brought in Shane Clifford to lead its global wealth business, followed by Bill Ryan for retirement solutions. Carlyle now puts the addressable family office market at approximately USD 5 trillion and says it has raised roughly USD 50 billion from individuals and wealthy families since its founding. The firm is targeting more than USD 200 billion of new capital through 2028, with USD 90 billion of that earmarked for its credit business alone.

The logic is structural rather than opportunistic. As traditional institutional channels, pension funds and endowments among them, face their own constraints on new allocations to private markets, alternative asset managers are turning to affluent individuals and family offices as the next source of scale, building dedicated servicing teams, co-investment structures and reporting designed for a single family rather than a committee. It is a mirror image of the shift J.P. Morgan's own family office survey described this week: institutions professionalising to meet families, just as families have been professionalising to meet institutions.

For the household side of a family's affairs, the significance is less about the capital than about who now sits at the table. A family office that used to deal with a handful of relationship managers is increasingly served by dedicated global teams built specifically around its profile, complete with named leadership and public growth targets. Estate managers and chiefs of staff who coordinate with the family office on payroll, property and logistics are likely to find that side of the relationship becoming steadily more institutional, structured and metric driven.
lead.why: As the largest alternative asset managers build dedicated global teams to win family offices as clients rather than treat them as occasional co-investors, the professionalisation reaching the investment side of a family's affairs increasingly sets the tone the household side is expected to match.

articles.title: Rents for the ultra wealthy in prime central London have risen by more than two thirds this year, Beauchamp Estates finds, as buyers turn tenants amid Gulf instability and Britain's post non dom tax regime
articles.body:
Beauchamp Estates' Millionaires Letting in London survey, published on 22 September, puts the average annual rent paid by an ultra high net worth tenant in prime central London at around GBP 220,000. Rents for luxury houses and mansions have risen 67.15 per cent over the year, to GBP 4,177 a week, or GBP 217,204 annually, up from GBP 2,499 a week in 2025. Luxury apartments and penthouses have climbed a more modest but still sharp 15.12 per cent, to GBP 1,957 a week, from GBP 1,700 a week the year before.

The standout lettings this year include a Mayfair house on Mount Street at GBP 33,000 a week, or GBP 1.71 million annually, a Chelsea townhouse on Cheyne Walk at GBP 30,000 a week, and a One Hyde Park apartment in Knightsbridge at GBP 32,500 a week. Beauchamp attributes the surge to falling supply set against rising demand, with applications from Middle Eastern tenants up 30 per cent over the year, American applicants up 20 per cent and Chinese applicants up 5 per cent. The agency links the Gulf figure directly to regional instability, describing London as a safe haven for wealthy Middle Eastern families choosing to rent rather than commit to a purchase.

A companion survey from Spear's, updated on 26 September, helps explain why renting has become the more attractive option for some. More than 80 per cent of the property advisers it polled rated lifestyle and schooling, not tax treatment, as the strongest driver of a purchase, and while Dubai ranked highest for pure desirability, Valletta and London led for investment potential. Eighty one per cent of the same advisers backed introducing professional licensing for London's super prime brokers, on American lines, a sign the market they operate in has outgrown its old, informal structure.

A family renting rather than owning changes the terms on which household staff are engaged. Leases run on different timelines to freehold ownership, a change of landlord can unsettle staffing arrangements built around a specific property, and portable staff who move with the family rather than stay with the house become more valuable than ever. The rental surge in London is, in that sense, also a surge in demand for private staff who can be redeployed at short notice.
articles.why: As more ultra wealthy families choose to rent rather than buy in London, the household staff built around a single freehold address are giving way to staff hired to move with the family itself, a shift agencies and estate managers are only beginning to plan around.
articles.src: Beauchamp Estates, via Letting Agent Today

articles.title: Discretion outranks every formal qualification in the American household staffing market, Morgan and Mallet's analysis of 465 job briefs finds, appearing in three times as many requests as certifications
articles.body:
Morgan and Mallet International has published an analysis of 465 household job briefs handled across the United States between May 2022 and June 2026, covering more than 27 states. Discretion and confidentiality appear as a requirement in 61.3 per cent of all briefs, roughly three times more often than formal qualifications or certifications, which appear in 20.4 per cent. Prior experience in a private household is specified in 58.5 per cent of briefs, ahead of practical skills such as laundry and ironing at 43.2 per cent, cooking at 41.3 per cent and events and entertaining at 31.6 per cent.

Nanny roles account for the largest single share of briefs, at 19.1 per cent, followed by housekeepers at 16.8 per cent, then private chefs, house or estate managers and personal assistants. Geographically, three states account for 63.2 per cent of all briefs: California at 24.1 per cent, Florida at 23.0 per cent and New York at 16.1 per cent, with New York City, Miami and Los Angeles the leading cities. The single largest shift in the data is Braselton, Georgia, a small town whose share of national briefs rose 8.0 percentage points in 2025, the largest gain recorded anywhere in the country.

The employment terms behind those briefs are notably stable. Full time roles account for 95.2 per cent of specified positions and permanent roles for 93.3 per cent, while live in arrangements make up 39.6 per cent against 32.5 per cent live out and 28.0 per cent open to either. Minimum experience requirements run highest for butlers and formal service roles, at an average of 6.7 years, ahead of estate management at 6.3 years and childcare at 4.7 years. Among briefs specifying language ability, English appears in 75.8 per cent, French in 26.8 per cent and Spanish in 25.5 per cent, while specialist skills such as fine dining or Michelin experience, at 7.5 per cent, and yacht experience, at 5.2 per cent, remain comparatively rare.

The dataset puts a number, for the first time at this scale, on something recruiters and household staff themselves have long said informally: trust is the primary credential in private service, well ahead of technical training. For a student entering the profession, it is also a map of where demand actually concentrates, both by role and by geography, including in places, like Braselton, that would not appear on an obvious shortlist.
articles.why: Quantifying discretion as the single most requested trait in private service, ahead of any technical qualification, confirms what the craft has always taught informally and gives it, for the first time, a number a student can point to.

articles.title: Four Geneva watch auctions open within three days this November, led by Phillips' Geneva Watch Auction XXIV, after a spring and summer in which Hong Kong sale totals rose 90 per cent year on year
articles.body:
Geneva's autumn watch auctions fall across three days this year: Phillips holds The Geneva Watch Auction XXIV alongside Antiquorum's Important Modern and Vintage Timepieces sale on 7 and 8 November, Sotheby's holds its live Important Watches sale on 8 November, and Christie's closes the week with Rare Watches Including Watches for ELA on 9 November. Together the four houses make Geneva, once again, the fixed point of the collecting calendar even as the market's centre of gravity keeps shifting east.

The results feeding expectations into November were set earlier in the year. A first series Patek Philippe reference 2499 sold for approximately USD 10.2 million in Hong Kong in May, an F.P. Journe Tourbillon Souverain, nicknamed Chine 2010 38, made roughly USD 4.2 million the same month, and a unique white gold Cartier Cheich sold for close to USD 3.4 million in Hong Kong in September. Trade publication Haute Time describes Hong Kong's spring and summer auction totals as up 90 per cent year on year.

Three patterns are shaping the market ahead of the Geneva sales: rarity and one off commissions are commanding outsized premiums over even well known references, independent watchmakers continue to outperform pre sale expectations, and blue chip vintage Patek Philippe remains, in the trade's own words, the market's reserve currency. For the private service world, the pattern that matters most is logistical rather than aesthetic. Single pieces now regularly worth seven or eight figures move between family houses, bank vaults and travelling exhibitions, and it is increasingly a house manager or personal assistant, not the auction house, who arranges the insurance, the transport and the provenance paperwork that follows a watch from the sale room to the safe.
articles.why: As individual watches trade for eight figure sums and move constantly between houses, vaults and exhibitions, the private staff responsible for a family's collection are taking on logistics and provenance work that once belonged to the auction house alone.

briefs.b: UBS's Trends in Philanthropy 2026, drawn from its Global Family Office Report, finds 41 per cent of family offices worldwide now treat philanthropy as their primary channel for impact, ahead of operating businesses at 30 per cent and investment portfolios at 26 per cent. Of those managing giving in house, 68 per cent are building their own impact expertise rather than outsourcing it, and 27 per cent are folding philanthropy into the family's wider affairs rather than keeping it in a separate foundation.

briefs.t: The world's largest yacht, on schedule
briefs.b: REV Ocean, the 194.9 metre explorer vessel built at Norway's Vard for Kjell Inge Rokke, is expected for delivery in the fourth quarter of 2026 and will become the largest superyacht afloat at 19,235 gross tons. Among roughly ten major deliveries due before the year is out, Amels' 120 metre Project Tanzanite will become the largest Dutch built motor yacht in history, and Lurssen's 114.2 metre Project Cosmos will cruise up to 1,000 nautical miles on twin 500 kilowatt methanol fuel cells.

In Spear's 2026 survey of the advisers who serve super prime buyers, more than 80 per cent rated lifestyle and schooling as the strongest driver of a purchase, ahead of tax treatment. Dubai ranked highest for pure desirability, with 69 per cent of experts scoring it 4 or 5 out of 5, while Valletta and London led on investment potential. Eighty one per cent of the same experts backed introducing professional licensing for London's super prime brokers, along American lines.
